titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Thursday, 21 September 1922
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
Dear Miss Weaver: I have just telegraphed to you asking you not to send out any of the enclosed circulars and I have asked Miss Beach not to do so at this end. I have a great objection to any association of my name or my book with the bookshop which has been suddenly substituted for that of
Messrs Emile Paul. I do not wish to be involved in any controversy concerning the aims and talents of the writers who have their headquarters there except to say that I strongly urge an immediate cancelling of the name. I hope that not many of the circulars have gone out.

I enclose also a letter from Mr Darantière by which it would seem that it was decided to go ahead with the printing already twelve days ago and apparently without any mention of the revision of the text. The letter from Mr Rodker alludes again to a ‘Paris agent’. I cannot understand what it means.
If any sum is involved for rent to the bookshop in my opinion it would be better to sacrifice it than to allow this plan to go forward.

closer.salute: In great haste and with kindest regards

div.note: John Rodker had found an office at La Librairie Six, a bookshop run by Philippe Soupault’s wife, where Man Ray had had a controversial “dada” exhibition. Rodker must have given that address on the first version of the flyer and JJ did not want to be associated with surrealism.

In earlier letters (e.g. to Ludmila Savitzky, 24 September 1920), JJ referred to the Paris publishing house Émile-Paul Frères as “Emile Paul”. They had shown an interest in acquiring the rights to Ulysses (Leonid Livak, “‘A Thankless Occupation’: James Joyce and His Translator Ludmila Savitzky”, JSA [2013], 33-61).

JJ encloses a typed letter from the printer, Maurice Darantiere, to Sylvia Beach, dated 11 September 1922, in which he notifies her that the printing of the second edition of Ulysses “pour Miss Weaver de Londres” has started that day. For this Egoist Press edition, he used the plates of the first edition.

The second edition of Ulysses (“Published by the Egoist Press, London, by John Rodker, Paris”) was printed in Dijon from the original plates, which the Egoist Press bought from Sylvia Beach. It came out in the weeks following this letter, on 12 October 1922.

In an enclosed letter from John Rodker to Sylvia Beach, dated 20 September 1922, Rodker writes that he is glad she is “thinking seriously” of his suggestion “that you should become the Paris agent” of the first British edition of Ulysses. The same day (20 September), JJ had already written to Weaver that Sylvia Beach was “bewildered by the words ‘Paris agent’ as she understood that that was Mr Rodker’s position” (LI 186).
